findings.statement: Section 12.4 and NFR-6 keep the CVC encrypted after authorization, until settlement or for up to 72 hours, and reuse it for incremental authorizations. They justify this by saying PCI DSS v4.0 Req. 3.2.1/3.3.2 allow SAD to be kept until the transaction is settled. Our understanding is that those clauses cover SAD stored only before authorization completes, and that keeping it after authorization is not allowed for a non-issuer service provider. If that is right, both the confirmed CVC decision and NFR-6 fail the Level 1 assessment that NFR-5 requires. This is unverified here and must be checked against the standard's text.
findings.title: CVC retention until settlement rests on a likely misreading of PCI DSS

evidence.quote: Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region.
Replication is storagelevel and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second.
With asynchronous replication, the RPO on region loss equals the replication lag at the time of failure (about 1 s, roughly 2,000 payments at peak), not zero.

next_step.action: Choose between relaxing NFR-4 with compensating reconciliation or funding synchronous cross-region commit.
next_step.owner: Head of Payments Platform / risk owner

recommendation.change_summary: The accountable owner chooses one of two options. (a) Restate NFR-4 as RPO ≤ the replication-lag SLO (for example 5 s) for regional loss and zero for AZ loss, and add a post-failover reconciliation step to 20.2 that rebuilds missing payments from acquirer and settlement records. (b) Add synchronous cross-region commit for authorizations, and budget its latency in 21.1. Update the NFR-4 acceptance criterion to match.
recommendation.expected_benefit: The DR objective becomes one that can be met and verified, and post-failover recovery of lost transactions is explicit.
recommendation.issue: NFR-4 and the DR design contradict each other.
recommendation.rationale: Ledger data lost without anyone knowing breaks P1 and P5 and causes reconciliation disputes.
recommendation.verification: Run a DR game day under load, measure the lost-write window, and confirm the recovery procedure restores the missing postings.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings even if the whole region is lost. The chosen DR mechanism, however, replicates asynchronously with sub-second lag, so writes committed in the last second before the region is lost can disappear. That means authorizations the merchant has already been told about, and their ledger postings, could be lost. The NFR-4 game-day criterion ('every posting committed... present') will fail on an unplanned failover, or else it will only pass when the test happens to fall in a quiet window.
findings.title: Zero regional RPO cannot be met with asynchronous Aurora Global Database

findings.statement: Section 9.3 says a single partition sustains 10,000 WCU/s and concludes that M-0001's ~1,800 WCU fits 'comfortably'. We believe the per-partition write limit is much lower (about 1,000 WCU/s). A table with an LSI also keeps each partition key's item collection in one partition with a size cap, which stops it from being split for heat. In addition, items carrying a response body of up to 4 KB use more than one WCU per write. If our belief about the limits holds, the idempotency layer will throttle the largest merchant at campaign peaks, putting FR-5 and NFR-1 at risk. These limits are unverified here.
findings.title: DynamoDB per-partition limit and hot merchant key capacity claim likely wrong

The trigger of 'second HSM at 1,500 TPS' and the 20 ms unwrap figure rest on an unstated vendor benchmark, not on measured HSM throughput at peak card volume.
